articles.title: Apple Begins Opening Siri AI to Developers
articles.summary: Apple Developer: Starting today with the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 betas, a new Developer Preview enables any developer to integrate their app with Siri AI, giving businesses and developers new ways to reach and serve their customers. [...] This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers. With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers.
articles.full_text:
Siri AI is now open to all developers November 3, 2026 Starting today with the iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 betas, a new Developer Preview enables any developer to integrate their app with Siri AI, giving businesses and developers new ways to reach and serve their customers.

Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri that is profoundly more capable, conversational, and personal, is designed to be deeply integrated into Apple’s operating systems and the apps people use every day, including the apps from our vast ecosystem of developers.

Thousands of developers have already built integrations with Siri to let users ask for directions, manage a to-do list, send a message, or catch up on an audiobook.

Siri AI is available in many languages, including English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish and will soon expand to support Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

People around the world are turning to Siri AI to get things done every day, which means more customers can discover and use apps just by asking.

Today’s preview allows any app to bring its content and actions directly into Siri AI by using App Intents, making it easier for all apps to tap into Siri AI’s newest capabilities, including personal context understanding, onscreen awareness, natural language, and more.

So people can just ask for help in their own words, and Siri AI carries out any custom action you’ve built, from checking a delivery to booking a reservation to placing an order.

For complex requests, we’re also introducing skills to let you teach Siri AI how to combine several actions into a single experience.

And Siri AI can now surface any entity in the Spotlight semantic index, not just the ones that fit an existing schema.

We started rolling out these new capabilities across many Apple apps, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather, so users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year.

There are many more actions available now as examples for you to reference.

To see what you can do in each app, just ask Siri AI.

This developer beta offers a sneak peek at Siri AI app intents for developers.

With this early Developer Preview, your app can work directly with Siri AI, giving you a first look at new ways to reach and serve your customers.

This preview provides early access before first shipping to customers in a few months; and with submission to the App Store opening up in the spring, developers have time to explore, build, and help shape their experiences before launch.

Try it out and share your feedback.

As you explore early, we will follow up with more details about the terms and usage policies for experiences enabled through Siri AI.

More to share soon.

To learn more about the new APIs, how to use them, and how to evaluate your app’s experience with Siri AI, read new documentation .

You can also connect with Apple engineers in Apple Intelligence Group Labs on November 4–5 to ask questions, get advice, and follow the discussion.

Sign up for November 4, 9–10 a.m. (PT) Sign up for November 5, 6–7 p.m. (PT) Siri AI is available in beta in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, watchOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3 and requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled device set to a supported language.

It is available in English, French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Some features may not be available in all regions or languages.

Siri AI is currently unavailable in the EU in iOS, iPadOS, and watchOS.

Apple is working constructively with the EU in an attempt to find a path forward.

Siri AI is not available for users under 13.

Certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side models are subject to daily usage limits, including but not limited to Siri AI, intelligent photo editing tools, Image Playground, and AFM 3 Cloud models in Shortcuts.

Daily limits may vary by feature, request complexity, system demand, system policies, and other factors.

Expanded access to such features will be available for a fee in the future.

Use of these features is subject to the Apple Intelligence terms and conditions.

Learn more at support.apple.com/148587.

articles.title: Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
articles.summary: Called FlashProve, the system would let anyone check that an AI response really came from the model it claims to be from.
articles.full_text:
Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday.

The system, called FlashProve , is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model.

It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using.

Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model.

In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results.

FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?” To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically.

Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private.

That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too.

The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device.

As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub .

Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab. “This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.” Topics AI , Anthropic , cryptography , inference When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

articles.title: OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
articles.summary: In many circles, "Ask Chat" has replaced "Google it," and that's reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google. Adam Fry, OpenAI's consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. He said […]
articles.full_text:
AI Report Tech OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search ChatGPT processes one-fifth the volume of search queries as Google, per OpenAI.

ChatGPT processes one-fifth the volume of search queries as Google, per OpenAI. by Hayden Field Nov 3, 2026, 6:30 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Hayden Field is The Verge’s senior AI reporter.

An AI beat reporter for more than five years, her work has also appeared in CNBC, MIT Technology Review, Wired UK, and other outlets.

In many circles, “Ask Chat” has replaced “Google it,” and that’s reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google.

Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday.

He said the company defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to tasks like defining a term or a simple how-to explanation. (Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.) Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade.

During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it — now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.) The news comes amid an ongoing search engine shake-up, as Google continues to reduce conventional referrals to third-party sites and invests heavily in AI tools — not just AI Overview but also additional generative AI capabilities , including personalized search results with visualizations and charts.

But as search queries increasingly route through OpenAI and other AI labs’ services, other companies are investing in the same types of AI-focused search experience, even if they call it something else: for OpenAI, it’s “Intelligent UI,” or creating a visual and interactive interface within a chatbot response. “That’s where the future of this technology goes.

You’re talking to a canvas,” Fry said.

Much like Google, OpenAI sees a potential path to profitability through ads, particularly as it approaches an IPO potentially slated for early next year.

OpenAI has defended its ads in the past, and Fry told reporters they hadn’t produced a lasting backlash. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, adding that “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.” OpenAI announced last month that the company would begin introducing images of sponsored products and services in ChatGPT rather than just a company’s name, logo, and a link to its product like before. “Ads have maybe shown us that we could be doing this more, actually,” Fry said.

articles.title: Anthropic is still grappling with the economics of compute
articles.summary: At a moment when Anthropic's compute margins should be getting better, they’re getting worse.
articles.full_text:
There’s a lot of mystery around the finances of major AI labs, and as Anthropic inches towards it IPO, we’re starting to get some answers.

In particular, the company is finally disclosing more about the economics of compute, and how much of Anthropic’s skyrocketing revenue is being lost to compute costs.

In a new filing on Monday , Anthropic released data that showed those margins on compute actually getting worse.

The filing was an update to the S-1 released last week — but where that filing’s financial disclosures only covered through June 30 of this year, the new data extended to disclose results through an extra quarter, to September 30.

Broadly, Anthropic had a good quarter: revenue reached $17 billion, up from $11.5 billion in the previous quarter, suggesting durable growth.

But the operating loss grew at the same time, thanks in large part to growing compute costs.

Looking at the compute margins makes the picture even worse.

In the new quarter, compute took up 58% of the company’s revenue, up from 48% the quarter before.

At a moment when the company could win over IPO investors by showing margins improving, they’re getting worse.

A chart in the filing shows this even more clearly, tracking the company’s revenue for every dollar spent on compute.

Since the start of 2025, it’s been steadily growing, peaking at just over 2x this past quarter, then falling back down to 1.72x.

Many indications imply that this shift in compute margins is more of a blip than a long-term problem, but it still tells us important things about the business of running a major lab.

Trying to keep up with demand, Anthropic’s compute bill shot up to $10 billion for the quarter, including, as the filing notes, “$5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments, which currently costs significantly more than comparable compute procured under our multi-year commitments.” Basically, demand was growing so fast that Anthropic had to scramble for compute, which meant paying higher rates.

Some of those deals have already played out in public.

Anthropic has been paying SpaceX $1.25 billion a month for compute, alongside multibillion-dollar deals with Nscale , Akamai , and Volta .

In the parlance of the industry, these are neoclouds rather than hyperscalers — smaller outfits that offer more flexible compute deals at higher rates.

Anthropic’s margins got worse in Q3 because of deals like these, and there’s no sign they’ll be able to do without them anytime soon.

As the new filing puts it, “We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain our largest operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute.” Anthropic is still trying to lower its compute costs.

In particular, the company talks quite a bit about its efforts to build its own compute base under a project it calls “Anthropic Direct.” But with demand growing so fast, those efforts aren’t going to be able to keep pace, and the neoclouds will continue to be the best option they have.

In a sense, these are champagne problems.

As long as revenue is growing at nearly 50% a quarter, few investors will worry about high compute costs — and the moment demand slows down, investors may be comforted by a compute picture that has gotten a lot sunnier.

But it’s a reminder of how much AI labs still depend on the trillion-dollar infrastructure buildout — and how vulnerable they are to hiccups in that process.

It’s easy to imagine the data center buildout slowing down over the next year if bond markets get skittish or local opposition gets more intense.

There’s not much Anthropic can do to address either of those risks, and either one would make a messy compute picture a whole lot messier.

In the meantime, the future of Anthropic and other labs will be at the mercy of compute prices.

articles.title: Google is entirely disabling Search in schools that don’t want AI
articles.summary: Google is completely turning off Search in schools that reject its AI features, the company told The New York Times. The decision was also shared in a broader education-related update from Google on Tuesday, saying that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search "will be entirely off" for K-12 student accounts […]
articles.full_text:
Tech AI News Google is entirely disabling Search in schools that don’t want AI Students in schools that reject Google’s AI will see notices that Search isn’t available.

Students in schools that reject Google’s AI will see notices that Search isn’t available. by Emma Roth Nov 3, 2026, 5:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: The Verge Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Google is completely turning off Search in schools that reject its AI features, the company told The New York Times .

The decision was also shared in a broader education-related update from Google on Tuesday, saying that access to Gemini, Gemini Notebook, Gemini in Classroom, and Google Search “will be entirely off” for K-12 student accounts unless “administrators explicitly turn them on.” Administrators will not be given the option to toggle Gemini-powered features off without disabling Search, however.

Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the NYT , “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” adding that schools that disable Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search, and they’ll see a message from their school that indicates it’s not available.” Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for comment.

Related Schools are catching on to Big Tech’s playbook NYC bans AI use for students until they reach high school The announcement comes just months after Google turned its Gemini AI assistant on by default inside the Google Classroom app, which is used by more than 150 million teachers and students globally.

The move added to skepticism surrounding Google’s introduction of AI in schools amid reports of declining test scores and other impacts on students’ learning abilities .

Last month, lawmakers pressed Google on the “potential harms” of putting its AI products in schools.

Although Google is no longer turning on AI features in schools by default, this choice comes at a cost.

Several lawmakers and local leaders have responded to Google’s move to block Search, with Sen.

Bernie Sanders (D-VT) calling it “extortion” and NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani saying , “no corporation should have the power to dictate how we teach our children.” Rohit Chopra, California’s Secretary of Business & Consumer Services, wrote that Big Tech shouldn’t be able to “strong-arm schools.” Google argues that this change will “give schools more choice, not less,” adding that schools can choose to turn off each service on or off individually.

The company is also attempting to address concerns about students using its AI features to find “shortcuts” instead of solving problems themselves.

Google is embedding its Guided Learning feature, which is supposed to help students work through problems , into its AI Overviews in Search.

Google will begin testing this feature in select US schools this month.

Update, November 3rd: Added responses from lawmakers and Google.
